A Hierarchical Graph Attention Encoder is designed for efficient state encoding, and the optimization process is formulated as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process for adaptive sequential decision-making. Extensive experiments and ANSYS ® Mechanical-based engineering validation on two benchmark structures confirm the framework’s superiority over established methods: the GNN-D3QN-optimized mesh reduces stress estimation error by 48.79% (reaching a low absolute relative error of 4.67%) for the perforated beam benchmark, delivers a 45.15% solver speedup for the L-shaped stress singularity bracket, and all optimized meshes meet strict geometric validity requirements and produce physically plausible stress distributions. This work establishes a unified data-driven closed-loop framework for simulation workflow automation. By integrating artificial intelligence with computational geometry, the proposed method improves simulation fidelity and efficiency while reducing manual intervention, offering a scalable foundation for next-generation adaptive simulation systems.

title: Transition-aware learning for surrogate modeling of expensive engineering response surfaces
abstract: Active learning methods for Gaussian-process regression typically focus on reducing global uncertainty or balancing exploration with exploitation. In many scientific and engineering applications, however, the main difficulty in surrogate modeling lies in localized transition regions where the response changes rapidly. These regions often govern threshold detection, regime identification, and local sensitivity, yet standard acquisition rules, such as maximum predictive variance and upper confidence bound, may not allocate samples efficiently in regions where such structural changes occur. This paper introduces Transition-Aware Learning (TAL), a novel Gaussian-process active-learning strategy designed specifically for transition-rich response surfaces. TAL combines predictive uncertainty with transition-sensitive posterior indicators derived from the evolving surrogate, including gradient- and curvature-related quantities in one dimension and their natural extensions in two dimensions. In this way, the method preferentially samples locations where epistemic uncertainty and local structural change coincide, directing evaluations toward the most informative transition zones while remaining fully sequential and computationally comparable to standard Gaussian-process baselines. TAL is evaluated against random sampling, maximum predictive variance, and Gaussian-process upper confidence bound on a benchmark suite of six one-dimensional synthetic engineering-style response surfaces and two two-dimensional extension cases. The one-dimensional suite spans transition-rich behaviors, including stall-like drops, smooth regime switches, saturation knees, piecewise shoulders, multiple transitions, and oscillation-gated responses. At the same time, the two-dimensional cases test whether the same sampling principle remains effective when the dominant feature is a transition contour rather than a point. A sensitivity study is additionally used to assess robustness to the relative weighting of the uncertainty, gradient, and curvature terms, and an experimental NACA 0012 lift dataset provides an engineering demonstration of active reconstruction near aerodynamic stall. Performance is assessed using both global and transition-focused metrics, including root-mean-square error, transition-location error, transition-band error, and transition-mask intersection-over-union. Across the one-dimensional benchmark suite, TAL achieves the lowest average final transition-location error and the lowest average final root-mean-square error while remaining computationally comparable to the strongest baselines. The weight-sensitivity study shows that these results are robust to moderate changes in the acquisition weights rather than depending strongly on the nominal weighting. In the two-dimensional extension cases, TAL remains competitive in both global and local transition-region accuracy. It consistently outperforms the upper confidence bound, although its advantage over maximum predictive variance is less uniform than in one dimension. On the experimental NACA 0012 data, TAL achieves the lowest aggregate final reconstruction error while maintaining competitive stall-angle localization, providing evidence that the transition-aware sampling principle extends beyond the synthetic benchmark suite. These results show that transition-aware acquisition provides a practical and effective alternative to standard active-learning rules when accurate resolution of structural change is a primary modeling objective.

title: Wave finite element method for calculating the dynamic behaviour responses of cyclically symmetric structures under arbitrary load and boundary conditions
abstract: The finite element (FE) method for axisymmetric and cyclic symmetric structures has been extensively developed and integrated into numerous commercial FE method software packages. Leveraging the periodicity of the geometry and loads, the dynamics of a 3D structure can be analysed by considering only a section or a single period, thereby reducing computation time. However, in cases where there is asymmetry in the boundary conditions and loading, the FE method presents certain limitations, particularly with regard to the computational time required for complex structural components. This article introduces a novel approach using the Wave Finite Element (WFE) method to calculate the dynamic responses of structures with non-symmetric loads and boundary conditions. By employing WFE for periodic structures, we can determine the wave decomposition of a substructure’s responses within a cylindrical coordinate system. The loads on the substructure are represented as waves added to the response. This wave decomposition is then applied to all substructures until reaching the first one, resulting in a relationship between the wave amplitudes and the external loads. This expression is simple and can accommodate non-symmetric boundary conditions applied to full or partial interface sub-parts, handled via a reaction-force approach. This paper presents two simple numerical examples, one in 2D and the other in 3D, to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in reducing calculation time compared to the classical FE method, while maintaining a small relative error.

title: Vibration and buckling analysis of variable-thickness FGM cylindrical shell panels with uncertainty quantification and GPR-based sensitivity
abstract: This study investigates the dynamic and stability behaviour of Functionally Graded Material (FGM) cylindrical shell panels with thickness variation using third order shear deformation theory based C⁰ finite element model. Open shallow cylindrical shells with tapered thickness profiles and different material gradation are analysed for free vibration, transient response, and linear buckling. Transient analysis is carried out using Newmark’s time integration scheme. The effects of key geometric and material parameters, including gradient index, thickness variation coefficient, radius to span ratio etc., on mechanical response of the shells are systematically examined. A maximum 142% rise in critical buckling load and 34% rise in frequency are observed due to the thickness variation coefficient \(\left(\delta \right)\) in the FGM shell. Uncertainty analysis reveals that power law graded shells show the largest variability (CV = 16.4% in vibration and 48.58% in buckling), whereas exponential gradation provides most robust response with the lowest variability (CV = 12.16–32.57%). Additionally, a Gaussian process regression (GPR) based permutation feature importance (PFI) and correlation analysis are employed to quantify the sensitivity of governing parameters.

title: A mesh-based neural energy solver for linear and nonlinear plane elasticity problems
abstract: This study presents a mesh-based neural energy solver (MNES) for linear and nonlinear elasticity on fixed finite-element discretizations. MNES is formulated as a neural reparameterization of a discrete finite-element energy problem, in which only the nodal displacement vector is parameterized by a coordinate-based neural network, while the finite-element mesh, interpolation, boundary conditions, and element energies remain fixed. The loss function is defined as the total potential energy of the discretized system, assembled element-wise from strain energy and external work, with element energies evaluated using the predicted nodal displacements and the prescribed finite-element interpolation. Unlike residual-based physics-informed neural networks and continuous-field deep energy methods, the loss function is constructed directly from the discretized finite-element energy without requiring spatial differentiation of the neural network outputs with respect to the input coordinates. Several benchmark problems in both linear and nonlinear elasticity are investigated to assess the proposed formulation. The results demonstrate that MNES accurately reproduces the corresponding finite-element energy solutions and highlight the potential of neural reparameterization as an alternative formulation for solving discretized finite-element variational problems.

title: Topology optimization for fluid–structure interaction with precise evolving boundaries using iso geometric analysis
abstract: Abstract We present a novel body-fitted iso geometric topology optimization framework for fluid–structure interaction problems. Using a spline-based parametric representation of the fluid and solid domains as well as their interface, the method enables consistent evaluation of flow and structural quantities on geometrically accurate boundaries throughout the optimization process. When verified on various benchmark problems, the underlying iso geometric analysis exhibited higher accuracy and superior convergence rates in comparison to standard finite element methods. A shape optimization stage is introduced after the optimized topology is obtained, alleviating geometric artifacts arising from trimming and untrimming operations and reducing computational effort while preserving geometric smoothness and convergence. Several numerical examples demonstrate the capabilities of the framework to optimize fluid–structure interactions involving challenging functionals such as lift, drag, pressure drop, interfacial stress and fluid-to-solid traction distribution. Overall, the framework provides an accurate and physically consistent approach for shape and topology optimization in fluid–structure interaction systems.

title: Me-fPINNs: multi-model ensemble fractional physics-informed neural networks for solving fractional integro-differential equations
abstract: Fractional integro-differential equations (FIDEs) play a pivotal role in modeling nonlocal and memory-dependent phenomena across scientific and engineering domains. While fractional physics-informed neural networks (fPINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative to conventional numerical methods, their reliance on single-network architectures often leads to limited accuracy, structural bias, and poor generalization under sparse data or high-dimensional settings. To address these limitations, this work proposes a Multi-Model Ensemble Fractional Physics-Informed Neural Network (Me-fPINNs), a novel soft computing framework that integrates five heterogeneous base models constructed from seven neural networks with diverse architectures, activation functions, and loss formulations. A key innovation lies in an operator-decoupled subnetwork design, which separately approximates fractional derivative and integral operators before adaptively fusing them through a nonlinear ensemble network. Extensive numerical experiments on one-dimensional linear/nonlinear, three-dimensional, and coupled fractional systems, as well as inverse problems, demonstrate that Me-fPINNs consistently outperform conventional fPINNs in accuracy stability, and robustness. As a mesh-free deep learning scheme, Me-fPINNs provide a promising solution for complex fractional modeling tasks in real-world applications.

title: Machine learning-based design of optimal explicit Runge–Kutta schemes for compressible flow equations
abstract: This study presents a novel artificial neural network (ANN)-assisted framework for developing adaptive optimized explicit Runge–Kutta (OERK) schemes for compressible flow simulations. Unlike existing optimized Runge–Kutta methods developed for either convection or diffusion-dominated regimes, the proposed approach incorporates the local Peclet number directly into the optimization process, enabling adaptive time integration across a broad range of flow conditions. Convex optimization is used to construct optimal stability polynomials for different Peclet numbers and temporal orders of accuracy. The resulting optimized coefficients are then used to train an ANN that predicts locally optimal Runge–Kutta coefficients without repeated optimization during simulations. The proposed methodology is validated using linear and nonlinear ordinary differential equations, one-dimensional convection–diffusion equation, laminar flow over a circular cylinder and turbulent flow around a NACA 0012 airfoil. Numerical results demonstrate that the ANN-predicted schemes preserve the desired order of accuracy while reproducing the optimized stability characteristics. For flow over cylinder case, computational cost reductions of 54–69% relative to classical Runge–Kutta schemes and 17–22% relative to previously optimized methods are achieved. For simulation of turbulent flow over airfoil, CPU-time reductions of 28–41% and 29–35% are obtained, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining convex optimization and machine learning to develop stable, accurate, and computationally efficient adaptive time-integration schemes.

title: Physics-informed Fourier basis neural network for fluid mechanics
abstract: Abstract Conventional machine learning approaches struggle to capture periodic patterns and solve quasi-periodic boundary problems in fluid mechanics. This study proposes a physics-informed Fourier basis neural network (PIFBNN) that integrates adaptive Fourier series with physical constraints to address canonical partial differential equations. The architecture preserves Fourier series' natural mathematical compatibility with periodic phenomena while incorporating trainable parameters (angular frequencies and weight coefficients) that enhance basis function flexibility and nonlinear learning capacity. We evaluate the framework on six fundamental fluid dynamics benchmarks: two-dimensional cylinder wake flow, lid-driven cavity flow, Kovasznay flow, Helmholtz equation, Burgers equation, and Allen-Cahn equation. Results demonstrate PIFBNN's consistent superiority over standard physics-informed neural network (PINN) in accuracy. Through sparse data reconstruction experiments and adjusting the activation functions of neural networks and comparing , we further validate the dual advantages of Fourier basis neural network (FBNN) over conventional artificial neural network (ANN): inherent periodicity handling and reduced sensitivity to activation function selection. The FBNN architecture maintains robust performance across different activation functions, as verified through systematic comparisons with ANN and PINN baselines. These findings position PIFBNN as a promising computational framework for complex fluid dynamics problems.

title: A serial multi-layer latent mapping-based multi-fidelity framework for time-dependent reliability analysis under mixed random–fuzzy uncertainty
abstract: To address the problem of time-dependent reliability analysis for high-cost engineering structures under mixed random–fuzzy uncertainty, a novel multi-fidelity framework is proposed by integrating a serial multi-layer latent mapping model (SMLM) with hyper-rectangular constrained subset simulation (HCSS). The proposed method employs SMLM to provide a unified characterization of the correlation structure among data of different fidelity levels, thereby enhancing the response approximation capability for mixed inputs involving random continuous variables and fuzzy state variables. Meanwhile, HCSS generates critical candidate samples layer by layer within constrained hyper-rectangular regions, enabling sequential surrogate updates in the vicinity of the failure boundary and thus improving the efficiency and accuracy of interval estimation for time-dependent failure probabilities. Numerical examples and the engineering case of a wing box structure demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively fuse multi-fidelity information and maintain high accuracy and stability in boundary estimation while significantly reducing the number of high-fidelity model evaluations.

title: Understanding surrogate modeling for reliability analysis: optimization versus active learning with a probability-aware SPLA metric
abstract: Surrogate modeling is widely used to reduce the computational cost of Monte Carlo simulation (MCS)-based reliability analysis involving expensive performance functions. However, the relative effectiveness of different surrogate construction strategies in reliability applications remains insufficiently understood. This study compares two major paradigms for surrogate modeling: optimization-based and active learning-based strategies, referred to as oMMs and iMMs. Three representative techniques—artificial neural networks, Gaussian process regression, and support vector regression—are implemented within these frameworks. To assess surrogate performance from a reliability perspective, a probability-aware sign-penalized limit-state accuracy (SPLA) index is proposed. The index emphasizes prediction accuracy near the limit-state surface and penalizes sign misclassification that directly affects failure probability estimation. Four structural and geotechnical examples are investigated. The results show that high global surrogate accuracy achieved by oMMs does not guarantee reliable failure probability estimates and often requires substantially higher computational cost. In contrast, iMMs consistently provide more accurate and stable reliability predictions by adaptively enriching training data near the limit-state surface, as reflected by higher SPLA values. Furthermore, SPLA is employed to guide the selection of reliable models in bootstrap-based bagging ensembles, enhancing the robustness of surrogate predictions while maintaining high reliability estimation accuracy.

title: Efficient finite element quadrature on immersed voxel data
abstract: Abstract High-resolution computed tomography (CT) scans provide voxel-wise information on geometry and material properties. Direct numerical simulations on CT data in which each voxel is considered a finite element can yield billions of unknowns, a resolution that is often excessive. Coarsening the finite element mesh reduces the number of unknowns, but accurate quadrature then becomes a challenge. Composed integration by distributing Gauss-Legendre points on each voxel is computationally expensive due to the resulting large number of integration points. The standard remedy is to pre-integrate the stiffness contribution of each voxel in reference coordinates. However, this approach does not directly extend to local enrichment of the finite element space. For example, under hierarchical octree-based refinement the basis functions vary from element to element. For such cases, we develop an efficient voxel quadrature scheme based on a modified moment-fitting approach. The method computes a custom integration rule for each element which absorbs voxel information directly into the integration weights. This enables exact integration of the stiffness matrix of finite elements with any polynomial degree while limiting the number of quadrature points during assembly. In contrast to pre-integration, our approach decouples the material resolution from the finite element basis and is even faster for coarse finite element resolutions, while remaining far cheaper than composed Gauss-Legendre quadrature. We demonstrate voxel-based moment fitting on three examples: a scaling analysis for heterogeneous voxel data, a voxelized L-shaped domain with adaptivity driven by a residual-based error estimator, and a locally refined phase-field fracture simulation.

title: Voronoi diagram-based volume decomposition and overhang control in topology optimization for multi-axis additive manufacturing
abstract: Abstract The paper proposes a partition-based topology optimization approach for multi-axis additive manufacturing(AM), aiming to fully leverage its advantages in dynamic build orientation adjustment and region-specific manufacturing. To address the challenge of decomposing the evolving structural layouts, an implicit decomposition method based on Voronoi diagrams is introduced, which employs a Softmax function combined with Heaviside projection. This Voronoi-based approach ensures full coverage of the design domain and hence provides stable partitioning for arbitrary geometries. Complex volume decomposition is achieved by controlling a small number of seed points within the Voronoi diagram. To prevent unrealistic diffuse interfaces between partitions, a Kreisselmeier–Steinhauser(KS) aggregation-based distance constraint is imposed on the seed points. By integrating the volume decomposition with the spatial gradient of the structural density field, global overhang constraints are formulated for individual partitions. We then optimize the topological layout, partitions and their associated build orientations simultaneously to obtain self-supported design in density-based topology optimization. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, several 2D and 3D numerical examples are studied. The influence of partitioning parameters, including the initial build orientations in partitions and the number of partitions, on the optimized design is investigated. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed method yields reasonable partitioned designs, with the overhang surfaces in the partitions effectively controlled.

title: Deep generative graphs for synthesizing microstructure of topology-preserved polymer-bonded explosives
abstract: We introduce a generative artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm trained to generate realistic three-dimensional microstructures of polymer-bonded explosives (PBX). We idealize PBX as a two-phase composite with anisotropic crystals as inclusions in a polymer matrix. To improve memory efficiency, we introduce a two-stage hierarchical algorithm in which a deep generative graph model captures the grain topology in the PBX, while a latent diffusion model generates the 3D geometry of individual grains. This approach enables us to idealize each grain as a simply connected body embedded in three-dimensional space. This divide-and-conquer strategy enables us to bypass the challenging task of generating manifolds of complex topology and to avoid wasted computations when applying convolutions to grids dominated by constant values. To generate PBX microstructures with realistic grain topology, we sample sub-domains of segmented micro-computed tomography (CT) images of a mock PBX with Idoxuridine (IDOX) grains to form a dataset. Each sub-domain is represented by a node-weighted graph with the position, size, and shape descriptors stored as node features. The topological dataset is then used to train a graph recurrent neural network (GraphRNN) that learns to add nodes and edges sequentially to form a weighted graph describing the IDOX granular network, consisting of nodes with features connected by edges. With the global topology prescribed, the individual grains are generated by a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model that takes node features as inputs and produces grains that match the prescribed node features. Numerical examples assess the similarity between the actual and synthetic microstructures.

title: Automated lattice embedding and transitioning with application to multi-lattice topology optimization
abstract: Abstract Structures composed of spatially-varying architected materials have great potential for targeted mechanical and/or multifunctional behavior, but lack of structural integrity at the interfaces between different architecture geometries can degrade the expected performance. While smooth transitions between functionally-defined architected materials can be designed easily using mathematical interpolation, a robust transitioning scheme is less apparent for architectures without a simple mathematical description. Here we focus on periodic, strut-based lattices exhibiting cubic symmetry of their nodes and propose an algorithm that automates the design of smoothly-varying transitions between any finite set of these lattices embedded in a macroscale structure. The algorithm takes in lattice existence and relative density fields indicating which lattice and associated relative density exists at each point in the macroscale structure, and an ordered set of $$m$$ key lattices to be embedded. We define a transitional skeleton (i.e., nodes and connectivity) that encapsulates all $$m$$ key lattices via a continuous morphing between different nodal configurations, and use it to spatially transition between the different lattice geometries. Material is added after manipulating the skeletons according to the given relative density distribution. We explain details of the algorithm in 2D using a multi-lattice design obtained from topology optimization and show the flexibility and robustness of the algorithm by generating a lattice-embedded rendering of The Starry Night by Vincent Van Gogh. In 3D, we explore the effect of the transition radius and demonstrate manufacturability of the spatially-varying lattice-embedded structures by 3D printing a multi-lattice canopy obtained from topology optimization.

title: Hybrid LRA constitutive model-driven FEM: small sample machine learning framework for evaluating four-point bending property of the laser deposition repaired TA15 short beam in aerospace
abstract: For the problems of scarce data, high cost and low efficiency in four-point bending property evaluation of the Laser Deposition Repaired TA15 short beam in aerospace, a Hybrid Constitutive Model Driven FEM - Small Sample Machine Learning framework is established to solve small sample scale issue in this study. Five Machine Learning model- ANN, SVR, GPR, RF and LSBoost were trained and compared by combining a novel K-Means Clustering-based data augmentation strategy (KMCE). the KMCE (Tangent core function) - GPR demonstrating superior accuracy and stability, achieving the lowest error ( < 1.4% ) across the ε-P curve and reducing computational time from 4800 s to 66 s. SHAP analysis identifies the distance from the loading position and the bottom edge length of the repaired zone as the most influential geometric parameters. Based on these findings, a regenerative repair concept is proposed, improving bending failure resistance by 13%. The framework provides an efficient, non-destructive evaluation tool for repaired aerospace thin-walled structures, with potential extension to other data-scarce simulation problems.

title: An XFEM-based moving refinement patch method for crack propagation
abstract: Accurate simulation of crack propagation by the extended finite element method (XFEM) is often limited by the high computational cost associated with global mesh refinement, or the need for predefined crack path. This paper presents an efficient alternative, namely an XFEM-based moving refinement patch method (MRPM). The main contribution is a penalty-based coupling scheme that connects a locally refined mesh patch with a coarse global mesh. With this formulation, the refinement patch can dynamically follow the propagating crack tip without re-meshing or prescribing the crack path in advance. In this way, the proposed method combines the accuracy of local mesh refinement with the computational efficiency of coarse-mesh discretization. The performance of the proposed method is assessed through several benchmark problems, including crack propagation in a beam under four-point bending and crack coalescence in a plate containing two separated cracks. The results show that MRPM can accurately capture both local fracture evolution and global structural response, while significantly reducing the computational cost compared with the classical XFEM.

title: FLOWS: a model to simulate water and solutes fluxes in agricultural and environmental systems. 1. Theory and applications with intercode benchmarking
abstract: Abstract FLOWS (FLOws of Water and Solutes in soils) is a dynamic physically-based model to simulate water flow and solute transport in the soil–plant–atmosphere system. The numerical code was written in MATLAB. One-dimensional vertical transient water flow is simulated by numerically solving the 1D form of the Richards equation (RE) using an implicit, backward, finite differences scheme with explicit linearization. As for the solutes, the code solves the 1D Advection Dispersion equation (ADE) by an explicit, central difference scheme, allowing for a relatively easy inclusion of non-linear adsorption and other non-linear processes. The model produces information on the time evolution of (among many other outputs): soil water contents and pressure potentials in the soil profile; solute (tracers, adsorbed, volatile and reactive solutes) concentrations in the soil profile; water and solute uptake and actual evapotranspiration for simulated crops; deep percolation water and solute fluxes; root uptake of water and solutes, also in presence of water and osmotic stresses; water fluxes and related solute fluxes to runoff; drainage water fluxes and related solute fluxes; irrigation fluxes computed by the model; and temperature in the soil profile. Compared to other existing models, some specificities of FLOWS model are: (1) integrated simulation of carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus transformations and transport contextually to the simulation of water contents and fluxes; (2) macroscopic root uptake; (3) irrigation management, by allowing to optimize the time scheduling and volumes according to some criterion based on the average pressure head in the root zone; (4) the possibility of running multi-site simulations, which may be especially important for spatially distributed simulations; and (5) an interactive graphical user interface, allowing the user to easily handle even large input files and seeing the simulation results by graphical display of the main output variables.

title: A physics-augmented machine learning constitutive model for damage in solids
abstract: We propose a data-driven constitutive framework for multidirectional damage mechanics for both compressible and incompressible materials. The formulation is thermodynamically consistent in the sense of satisfying the Clausius–Duhem inequality. The strain-energy density potentials are expressed as isotropic functions of the right Cauchy–Green deformation tensor and structural tensors that, together with the associated directional damage magnitudes, describe both inherent and damage-induced anisotropy. To guarantee the polyconvexity condition, non-decreasing convex neural networks with inputs that ensure polyconvexity are used to parameterize the strain energy density potentials. The model vanishes in the undeformed state, fulfilling the normality condition. In contrast to classical (1-d) damage models, the expressiveness of the new data-driven model is enhanced by employing a family of nonlinear, convex, decreasing functions to capture the effect of damage. The damage evolution is governed through damage potential where the corresponding damage threshold is in terms of the damage conjugate forces. Furthermore, the framework can predict damage-induced anisotropy in initially isotropic materials. To address the computational burden associated with training due to the dissipative nature of the problem, a decoupled training scheme is introduced. Model accuracy is demonstrated, first through synthetic benchmarks for incompressible isotropic, transversely isotropic, and compressible orthotropic materials, followed by a problem to test identifiability and, finally, validation against experimental data. The new data-driven model effectively captures the damage behavior of materials while adhering to the physical and mathematical constraints of constitutive modeling.
